topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: In the classic real estate progression of terms, which definition is broadest and includes the mere physical surface of the earth, along with the air above and the ground below, with no reference to ownership rights?
explanation: "Land" is the physical earth itself, including the surface, subsurface, and airspace, apart from any legal rights of ownership. "Real estate" adds man-made improvements attached to the land, and "real property" adds the bundle of legal rights of ownership on top of that.
source_note: Standard land / real estate / real property definitional hierarchy (real property law)

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: "Real estate" is generally distinguished from mere "land" because real estate also includes what?
choice_a: The legal bundle of ownership rights
choice_b: Man-made permanent improvements attached to the land, such as buildings and fences
choice_c: Only mineral deposits below the surface
choice_d: Only movable personal belongings on the site
explanation: Real estate is land plus the permanent, man-made improvements attached to it (buildings, fences, and similar structures). Adding the legal bundle of rights on top of real estate is what produces "real property."
source_note: Standard land / real estate / real property definitional hierarchy (real property law)

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: The set of legal rights that accompany ownership of real property -- including possession, control, exclusion, enjoyment, and disposition -- is commonly referred to by real estate educators as what?
explanation: The "bundle of rights" concept describes ownership of real property as a collection of separate legal rights -- like individual sticks in a bundle -- that can be separated, transferred, or limited individually (for example, by leasing away the right of possession while retaining the right of disposition).
source_note: Bundle of legal rights doctrine of real property ownership

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A property owner grants a neighbor a recorded easement to cross a corner of her lot, and also mortgages the property to a lender. Under the bundle-of-rights concept, what has occurred?
choice_a: The owner has lost her real property entirely
choice_b: The property has automatically converted to personal property
choice_c: The land has become government property under escheat
choice_d: Individual rights within the bundle (such as the right of exclusion and the right of control) have been partially transferred or encumbered while the owner retains the rest of the bundle
explanation: Because ownership is a bundle of separable rights, an owner can give away or encumber individual rights -- such as granting an easement (partially limiting the right to exclude) or pledging the property as loan collateral (limiting free disposition) -- without giving up the whole bundle.
source_note: Bundle of legal rights doctrine of real property ownership

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: Which of the following is one of the four widely recognized physical characteristics of land used in real estate and appraisal theory?
explanation: The four physical characteristics of land are immobility, indestructibility, non-homogeneity (uniqueness), and, in a broader sense, its fixed situs. Scarcity, permanence of investment, and area preference (situs) are instead economic characteristics of land.
source_note: Physical vs. economic characteristics of land (appraisal and real property theory)

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: No two parcels of real estate are ever exactly identical, even if they are the same size and shape, because each occupies a unique location on the earth. Which physical characteristic of land does this describe?
explanation: Non-homogeneity (uniqueness) reflects the legal principle that every parcel of land is one-of-a-kind because no two parcels can occupy the same physical location. This is one of the reasons courts will order specific performance for breach of a real estate sale contract.
source_note: Physical characteristics of land -- uniqueness/non-homogeneity (appraisal and real property theory)

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: "Area preference," also known by the term situs, is best described as which type of characteristic of land?
choice_a: A physical characteristic, because it describes the exact GPS coordinates of the parcel
choice_b: A legal characteristic created only by recorded covenants
choice_c: An economic characteristic, because it reflects the relative desirability of a location that drives value even though it isn't a physical trait
choice_d: Not a recognized real estate concept
explanation: Situs (area preference) is an economic characteristic of land: it captures the market's preference for one location over another, which directly affects value, even though it has no bearing on the land's physical attributes.
source_note: Economic characteristics of land -- situs/area preference (appraisal and real property theory)

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: Because land cannot be manufactured or increased in total supply, real estate professionals and appraisers describe land as having what economic characteristic?
explanation: Scarcity is an economic characteristic of land arising from the fact that the total supply of land is essentially fixed, which tends to support and increase land values as demand grows, especially in desirable locations.
source_note: Economic characteristics of land -- scarcity (appraisal and real property theory)

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A large capital investment in a building, such as a shopping center, tends to remain committed to that specific parcel for a very long period of time and cannot easily be moved or liquidated. This illustrates which economic characteristic of land?
explanation: Permanence of investment is an economic characteristic reflecting that once capital and labor are invested in developing land, that investment is fixed and difficult to recover quickly, which is part of why real estate financing is typically long-term.
source_note: Economic characteristics of land -- permanence of investment (appraisal and real property theory)

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A buyer wants to know whether the built-in wall oven, the custom-cut wall-to-wall carpet, and the freestanding microwave in the kitchen will convey with the sale of the home. Under general fixture law, which item is most likely to remain personal property (not automatically conveyed) absent a contrary agreement?
choice_d: None of them; all attached appliances are automatically real property
explanation: A freestanding countertop microwave is not physically attached (method of annexation) and is not custom-adapted to the specific space, so it remains personal property. The built-in oven and custom-fit carpet satisfy the annexation and adaptation tests for a fixture.
source_note: Fixture tests -- method of annexation and adaptation to realty

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: The common-law tests traditionally applied by courts to decide whether an item of personal property has become a fixture (and therefore real property) include all of the following EXCEPT:
choice_a: The method of annexation (how firmly the item is attached)
choice_b: The adaptation of the item to the use of the real estate
choice_c: The original purchase price the current owner paid for the item
choice_d: The intention of the party who installed the item at the time of installation
explanation: Courts weigh the method of annexation, the adaptation of the item to the property, the relationship of the parties, and the intention of the installing party (plus any express agreement) to decide fixture status. The item's original purchase price is not a recognized legal test.
source_note: Common-law fixture tests (annexation, adaptation, relationship, intention, agreement)

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: Of the traditional common-law fixture tests, which one is generally regarded as the most important, because the other factors (method of attachment, adaptation, and relationship of the parties) are largely used as evidence of it?
choice_b: The dollar value of the item
choice_c: The color or style of the item
choice_d: The intention of the party who installed or attached the item
explanation: Courts generally treat the installing party's intention as the controlling test, but that intention is inferred objectively from the surrounding facts -- such as how firmly the item is attached and how specifically it is adapted to the property -- rather than from later self-serving statements.
source_note: Common-law fixture tests -- intention as the primary factor

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A signed real estate purchase agreement expressly lists the dining room chandelier as an item of personal property that the seller will remove before closing, even though the chandelier is bolted to the ceiling. Which fixture rule governs here?
choice_a: A clear agreement between the parties controls fixture status and overrides the other common-law tests
choice_b: Method of annexation always overrides any contract language
choice_c: Chandeliers can never be fixtures under any circumstances
choice_d: The buyer automatically receives the chandelier regardless of the contract
explanation: An express agreement between the parties as to whether an item is included in or excluded from the sale controls over the other fixture tests. Buyers and sellers are free to contractually redefine which attached items convey with the real property.
source_note: Common-law fixture test -- express agreement of the parties controls

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A tenant who operates a dry-cleaning business installs specialized pressing equipment bolted to the floor of the leased commercial space. When the lease ends, who generally has the right to remove this equipment?
choice_a: The landlord, because anything bolted down automatically becomes a fixture owned by the landlord
choice_b: The tenant, because it is a trade fixture used in the tenant's business and is treated as personal property
choice_c: Neither party may remove it without a court order
choice_d: The equipment automatically escheats to the state
explanation: Trade fixtures are items a commercial tenant attaches to leased premises for use in a trade or business. Even though physically attached, trade fixtures remain the tenant's personal property and the tenant may remove them before the lease ends, generally with a duty to repair any resulting damage.
source_note: Trade fixture doctrine (landlord-tenant relationship exception to fixture rules)

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A farm tenant plants and cultivates a corn crop during the growing season, but the landlord unexpectedly terminates the tenancy before harvest through no fault of the tenant. Under the doctrine of emblements, what right does the tenant generally retain?
choice_a: No rights; the crop belongs entirely to the landlord once the tenancy ends
choice_b: The right to demand the landlord purchase the growing crop at full market value immediately
choice_c: The right to re-enter the land after the tenancy ends to cultivate and harvest the annually planted crop
choice_d: The right to convert the leased land into a fee simple estate
explanation: Emblements (fructus industriales) are annually cultivated crops produced by labor, classified as personal property of the tenant who planted them. The doctrine of emblements lets a tenant whose uncertain-duration tenancy ends without their fault re-enter later to harvest crops planted during the tenancy.
source_note: Doctrine of emblements (fructus industriales) -- annual crops as personal property

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: How does the law classify perennial trees, shrubs, and natural grasses growing on a parcel of land, in contrast to annually cultivated crops such as wheat or corn?
choice_a: Both are always classified as personal property
choice_b: Both are always classified as real property with no exceptions
choice_c: Perennial vegetation is personal property while annual crops are real property
choice_d: Perennial vegetation (fructus naturales) is real property, while annual crops (fructus industriales) are treated as personal property
explanation: Naturally occurring, perennial vegetation (fructus naturales) -- trees, grasses, and shrubs -- passes with the land as real property, since it does not require annual cultivation. Cultivated annual crops (fructus industriales), such as corn or vegetables, are treated as personal property (emblements) belonging to the party who planted them.
source_note: Fructus naturales vs. fructus industriales distinction (real vs. personal property)

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A landowner sells the airspace above her single-story building to a developer, who plans to construct additional stories on top without disturbing the existing structure or the land beneath it. This transaction illustrates which principle?
choice_a: Air rights can be severed from the underlying land and building and separately conveyed
choice_b: Air rights cannot legally be sold apart from the land
choice_c: This transaction converts the land into personal property
choice_d: The buyer automatically also acquires the subsurface mineral rights
explanation: Air rights are a distinct component of real property that can be severed and sold or leased separately from the surface and improvements below, subject to reasonable height limits and applicable aviation regulations -- a practice common with transferable development/air rights in dense urban areas.
source_note: Air rights as a severable real property interest

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A landowner's ownership of the airspace directly above her property is best described as which of the following?
choice_a: Unlimited in every respect, with no restrictions of any kind
choice_b: A recognized property right, but one that is limited by reasonable height and is subject to federal regulation of navigable airspace for aircraft
choice_c: Nonexistent; landowners have no rights to the air above their land
choice_d: Limited strictly to exactly 500 feet in every state
explanation: While a landowner has a real property right in the airspace above the land sufficient for reasonable use and enjoyment (such as constructing buildings), that right does not extend to the point of excluding aircraft lawfully using navigable airspace, which is federally regulated.
source_note: Air rights -- scope and limitation by navigable airspace regulation

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: Traditionally, ownership of land is described as extending downward from the surface to what point?
choice_a: A fixed 100 feet below the surface in every state
choice_b: No depth at all; subsurface rights always belong to the state
choice_c: Theoretically to the center of the earth (subsurface rights), subject to legal exceptions such as separately owned mineral or oil and gas rights
choice_d: Only as deep as any existing basement foundation
explanation: The traditional common-law maxim describes ownership of the subsurface as extending downward to the center of the earth, although in practice mineral, oil, and gas rights are frequently and lawfully severed from the surface estate and owned or leased separately.
source_note: Subsurface rights -- common-law extent of ownership below the surface

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A seller conveys a parcel of land by warranty deed but expressly reserves all oil, gas, and mineral rights for herself in the deed. After closing, who owns the mineral rights?
choice_a: The buyer, because mineral rights automatically transfer with the surface
choice_b: The state, because mineral rights cannot be privately owned
choice_c: The transaction is void because mineral rights cannot be reserved
choice_d: The seller, because mineral rights can be severed from the surface estate and retained separately by the grantor
explanation: Mineral rights (including oil and gas) are a severable component of the real property bundle. A grantor may convey the surface estate while expressly reserving the subsurface mineral estate, creating two separately owned property interests in what was one parcel.
source_note: Severance of mineral rights from the surface estate

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A homeowner's property borders a flowing, non-navigable stream. What category of water rights applies to this owner regarding the use of the stream's water?
explanation: Riparian rights apply to owners of land bordering flowing waters such as rivers and streams, generally allowing reasonable use of the water (for domestic, agricultural, or similar purposes) without unreasonably impeding its natural flow to downstream owners.
source_note: Riparian rights (flowing watercourses) vs. littoral rights

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A homeowner's lot borders a large, non-flowing natural lake. What category of water rights applies to this owner with respect to the lake?
explanation: Littoral rights apply to landowners whose property borders large, substantially non-flowing bodies of water, such as lakes, seas, and oceans, generally providing reasonable access to and use of the water.
source_note: Littoral rights (non-flowing bodies of water) vs. riparian rights

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: For a parcel bordering a non-navigable river, ownership of the underlying riverbed generally extends to what point, absent a contrary deed or statute?
choice_a: Not at all; the state always owns the bed of every river
choice_b: Only to the ordinary high-water mark, with the state owning the rest
choice_c: To the centerline (thread) of the non-navigable waterway
choice_d: To the far bank, granting ownership of the entire riverbed
explanation: For non-navigable bodies of water, the riparian owner typically holds title to the underlying land out to the centerline, or thread, of the waterway. For navigable waters, by contrast, the state typically holds the submerged land and the private owner's rights generally end at the ordinary high-water mark.
source_note: Riparian ownership boundary -- navigable vs. non-navigable waterways

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: Over many years, a slow, gradual deposit of soil carried by a river adds new land to the edge of a riparian owner's property. What is this process called, and who typically gains title to the new land?
choice_a: Avulsion; the state acquires the new land
choice_b: Escheat; the new land goes to the last known heirs
choice_c: Condemnation; the new land goes to the local government
choice_d: Accretion; the riparian owner typically acquires title to the newly deposited land
explanation: Accretion is the gradual, imperceptible addition of soil to land bordering a body of water through natural water action. Under long-standing common-law principle, the riparian or littoral owner acquires title to the accreted land as it forms.
source_note: Accretion -- gradual gain of land from natural water deposit

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A sudden flood event causes a river to abruptly shift its channel overnight, cutting through what used to be the middle of a farmer's field. How does the law typically treat the resulting change in the property boundary?
choice_a: This is avulsion, and the property boundary generally remains at the location of the original channel rather than moving with the river
choice_b: This is accretion, and the boundary immediately shifts to follow the river's new channel
choice_c: The land is automatically forfeited to the state under escheat
choice_d: The farmer immediately loses all riparian rights permanently
explanation: Avulsion is the sudden, perceptible loss (or relocation) of land caused by the rapid action of water, such as a flood suddenly changing a river's course. Unlike gradual accretion, avulsion generally does not shift the legal boundary, which stays fixed at the former channel location, and the affected owner typically retains a right to reclaim the land.
source_note: Avulsion -- sudden change in a watercourse does not shift the legal boundary

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: When a lake or pond gradually and permanently recedes, exposing new dry land along its former shoreline, this process and the resulting gain of land by the abutting owner is known by what term?
explanation: Reliction refers to the gradual, permanent recession of water (such as a shrinking lake) that exposes previously submerged land. Similar to accretion, the newly exposed land generally becomes the property of the abutting riparian or littoral owner.
source_note: Reliction -- gain of land from the gradual, permanent recession of water

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: Which legal description method identifies a property's boundaries by starting at a fixed point of beginning and proceeding around the parcel using a series of directions (bearings) and distances until returning to that same starting point?
explanation: Metes and bounds is the oldest legal description method used in the United States. It describes a parcel by walking its boundary from a fixed point of beginning (POB), using a sequence of courses (directions) and distances, and monuments, until the description closes back at the POB.
source_note: Metes and bounds legal description method

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: In a metes and bounds legal description, why must the sequence of calls ultimately return to the point of beginning (POB)?
choice_a: It is not actually required; descriptions may end anywhere
choice_b: It is only a stylistic tradition with no legal significance
choice_c: It is required only for parcels larger than 100 acres
choice_d: Returning to the POB is what closes the boundary and mathematically confirms the described tract forms a complete, enclosed parcel
explanation: A valid metes and bounds description must "close" -- that is, the final course and distance must return exactly to the point of beginning -- to legally and mathematically confirm that the calls describe a fully enclosed parcel of land rather than an open-ended line.
source_note: Metes and bounds -- requirement that the description close at the point of beginning

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A metes and bounds description contains a call referencing "an old oak tree," but a subsequent measured distance in the same description does not precisely reach that tree due to a surveying error. Under the traditional rules of construction for resolving conflicts in legal descriptions, which typically controls?
choice_a: The natural monument (the oak tree) generally controls over the measured distance
choice_b: The measured distance always controls over a natural monument
choice_c: The description is automatically void and unusable
explanation: When elements of a legal description conflict, courts traditionally give priority in this order: natural monuments, then artificial monuments, then distances, then directions, and lastly, area. A natural monument such as a specific tree generally controls over a conflicting measured distance.
source_note: Legal description conflict resolution -- monuments control over distances

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: In the government (rectangular) survey system, what two reference lines are used as the primary starting points for surveying a given region?
choice_a: A lot line and a block line
choice_b: A principal meridian (running north-south) and a base line (running east-west)
choice_d: A metes line and a bounds line
explanation: The rectangular (government) survey system is built around a principal meridian, a precisely surveyed north-south reference line, and a base line, a precisely surveyed east-west reference line, from which all townships and ranges in that survey area are measured.
source_note: Government (rectangular) survey system -- principal meridian and base line

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: In the government survey system, a standard township is how large, and how many sections does it contain?
explanation: A standard township under the government (rectangular) survey system is a 6-mile-by-6-mile square (36 square miles), subdivided into 36 numbered sections, each nominally one mile square.
source_note: Government (rectangular) survey system -- township dimensions and 36 sections

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: Under the government survey system, one full section of land measures one mile square and contains approximately how many acres?
explanation: A section is one square mile of land, which equals 640 acres. Sections are the basic unit of the rectangular survey system and are further subdivided into halves, quarters, and smaller aliquot parts for legal descriptions.
source_note: Government (rectangular) survey system -- one section equals 640 acres

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A legal description reads "the NE 1/4 of Section 14." Approximately how many acres does this parcel contain?
explanation: A quarter section is one-fourth of a full 640-acre section, which equals 160 acres (640 divided by 4). Quarter sections are one of the standard aliquot parts used in government survey legal descriptions.
source_note: Government (rectangular) survey system -- quarter-section acreage calculation

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A legal description reads "the SW 1/4 of the NW 1/4 of Section 22." Approximately how many acres does this parcel contain?
explanation: Each successive aliquot fraction is calculated by dividing the section (640 acres) by the denominator of each quarter in sequence: 640 divided by 4 (for the NW 1/4) equals 160 acres, and 160 divided by 4 (for the SW 1/4 of that quarter) equals 40 acres.
source_note: Government (rectangular) survey system -- aliquot part acreage calculation

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: Because the earth is curved and the government survey system's north-south range lines are designed to run true north, periodic east-west adjustment lines are needed roughly every 24 miles to correct for the resulting convergence of range lines. What are these adjustment lines called?
explanation: Because true north-south range lines converge toward the poles on a curved earth, the rectangular survey system uses correction lines (standard parallels), typically spaced at 24-mile intervals, to re-establish the full width of townships and keep sections close to their nominal 640-acre size.
source_note: Government (rectangular) survey system -- correction lines/standard parallels adjust for earth curvature

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A developer subdivides a large tract into individual home sites, records a map showing each numbered parcel grouped within numbered blocks, and files it with the county recorder. Buyers' deeds then describe their parcels by referencing this recorded map. What legal description method is being used?
explanation: The lot-and-block (recorded plat) system is commonly used for subdivided land. A surveyor prepares a plat map dividing the tract into numbered lots grouped into blocks; once recorded, individual parcels can be legally described simply by lot number, block number, subdivision name, and the recording reference.
source_note: Lot-and-block (recorded plat) legal description method

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A complete lot-and-block legal description typically must include which of the following elements?
choice_a: The lot number, block number, name of the subdivision, and the plat's recording reference (such as map book and page) in the applicable county records
choice_b: Only the street address of the property
choice_d: Only the buyer's and seller's names
explanation: A proper lot-and-block description identifies the specific lot and block, names the recorded subdivision, and cites where the plat map is officially recorded (for example, a map book and page number in the county recorder's or clerk's office), so the exact parcel can be located in the public record.
source_note: Lot-and-block (recorded plat) legal description -- required components

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: Which of the following would generally be considered an inadequate legal description for conveying real property in a deed?
choice_a: A metes and bounds description with a defined point of beginning
choice_b: A description consisting only of the property's mailing address
choice_c: A lot and block reference to a recorded subdivision plat
choice_d: A government survey description citing the section, township, and range
explanation: A mailing or street address alone is generally not considered a legally sufficient description for a deed, because it can change and does not precisely and permanently fix the boundaries of the parcel. Deeds require a description specific enough to locate the property without relying on outside oral testimony.
source_note: Legal sufficiency of property descriptions in deeds

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: To legally describe the vertical boundaries of an individual condominium unit -- such as the elevation of its floor and ceiling -- surveyors reference a fixed point of known elevation. What is this fixed reference point called?
explanation: A datum is an official, fixed reference elevation (often based on mean sea level) used to describe height or depth. Surveyors locate a datum on the ground using a benchmark, a permanent physical marker of known elevation, which is essential for describing multi-story or airspace interests such as condominium units.
source_note: Datum and benchmark -- elevation reference points for vertical (condominium) legal descriptions

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: What is the key functional difference between a "datum" and a "benchmark" as used in surveying and legal descriptions?
choice_a: There is no difference; the terms are perfectly interchangeable in every context
choice_b: A datum is used only for horizontal boundaries, and a benchmark only for property taxes
choice_c: A benchmark is a legal description method unrelated to elevation
choice_d: A datum is the official reference elevation itself (often mean sea level), while a benchmark is the physical, permanent marker placed on the ground that memorializes that known elevation
explanation: A datum is the abstract reference elevation point (commonly tied to mean sea level) against which height or depth is measured. A benchmark is the physical, permanent monument -- often a brass marker set in concrete -- that a surveyor places to mark and preserve a known point on that datum for future reference.
source_note: Distinction between a surveying datum and a physical benchmark

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A municipality enacts an ordinance limiting a residential zone to single-family homes, establishing minimum lot sizes, and imposing building setback requirements. Under what governmental authority is this type of zoning ordinance generally enacted?
explanation: Zoning ordinances are a classic exercise of a local government's police power -- its inherent authority to regulate private property use to protect public health, safety, and general welfare -- and generally do not require compensating affected owners since no property is physically taken.
source_note: Zoning as an exercise of police power (land use regulation)

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A small manufacturing plant was lawfully operating in a district before the city rezoned that area exclusively for residential use. The plant is allowed to continue operating despite no longer complying with the new zoning. What is this legal status called?
explanation: A legal nonconforming use, often called being "grandfathered in," occurs when a property's existing lawful use predates a new zoning ordinance that would otherwise prohibit it. The use may generally continue, though it is often subject to restrictions on expansion or rebuilding after destruction.
source_note: Nonconforming use ("grandfathering") under zoning law

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: An owner of an unusually shaped, narrow lot cannot meet the zoning ordinance's standard side-yard setback and build any structure at all on the lot. The owner petitions the zoning board for permission to build with a reduced setback due to this unique physical hardship. What is this type of relief called?
explanation: A variance is an authorized exception from the strict application of a zoning ordinance's requirements (such as setbacks or lot size), granted to a specific property owner who demonstrates unique physical hardship, as opposed to a nonconforming use, which involves a pre-existing lawful use rather than a newly requested exception.
source_note: Zoning variance -- hardship-based exception distinguished from a nonconforming use

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A city's zoning ordinance permits a use, such as a church or a daycare facility, in a residential district only after the operator obtains specific municipal approval addressing traffic, parking, and neighborhood compatibility. What is this type of approval commonly called?
choice_d: A conditional use permit (special use permit)
explanation: A conditional use permit (also called a special use permit) allows a use that is expressly recognized by the zoning ordinance as appropriate in a district, but only on a case-by-case basis subject to conditions, as distinguished from a variance, which excuses a use or structure that the ordinance would otherwise not permit at all.
source_note: Conditional use (special use) permit under zoning law

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A city council rezones a single small parcel in the middle of an established residential neighborhood to allow a gas station, without any comprehensive planning rationale connecting the change to the surrounding area. Real estate and land-use practice commonly refers to this improper, isolated rezoning as what?
explanation: Spot zoning refers to rezoning a small parcel in a way that is inconsistent with the surrounding area's comprehensive land use plan and appears to benefit a single owner rather than serve the general public welfare. Courts frequently strike down spot zoning as an arbitrary and improper exercise of the zoning power.
source_note: Spot zoning as an improper exercise of the zoning power

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: Property owner A owns a landlocked parcel with no direct access to a public road, and has a recorded right to cross a strip of neighboring property owner B's land to reach the highway. In this arrangement, which parcel is the "dominant tenement" and which is the "servient tenement"?
choice_a: A's parcel is servient; B's parcel is dominant
choice_b: A's parcel is dominant (it benefits from the easement); B's parcel is servient (it is burdened by the easement)
choice_d: Neither term applies because this is an easement in gross
explanation: In an easement appurtenant, the dominant tenement is the parcel that benefits from the easement (here, A's landlocked parcel), and the servient tenement is the parcel burdened by allowing the easement's use (here, B's parcel that is crossed).
source_note: Easement appurtenant -- dominant and servient tenement terminology

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: An easement appurtenant that benefits a dominant tenement will, absent a contrary agreement, do what when the dominant parcel is sold to a new owner?
choice_a: It automatically terminates upon the sale
choice_b: It must be renegotiated and separately re-recorded by the new owner
choice_c: It automatically transfers (runs) with the dominant parcel to the new owner
choice_d: It converts into an easement in gross
explanation: An easement appurtenant runs with the land -- it is attached to the dominant estate itself, not to a particular owner -- so it automatically passes to a new owner of the dominant tenement when that parcel is conveyed, without needing to be separately re-created.
source_note: Easement appurtenant -- runs with the land upon transfer

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A utility company holds a recorded right to maintain power lines across a property, but this right does not benefit any neighboring parcel of land -- it exists solely for the utility company's own personal benefit. What type of easement is this?
explanation: An easement in gross benefits a specific person or entity personally (commonly a utility, pipeline, or railroad company) rather than benefiting a dominant tenement. Because there is no dominant estate, an easement in gross does not automatically run with any parcel of land the way an easement appurtenant does.
source_note: Easement in gross -- personal easement with no dominant tenement

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A landowner subdivides a large parcel, and one resulting lot has no legal access to any public road except by crossing the seller's remaining land. Courts will often imply what type of easement in favor of the landlocked parcel, even without an express written grant?
explanation: An easement by necessity is implied by law (rather than expressly granted) when a landlocked parcel has no other reasonable access to a public road, typically arising when a single owner divides a tract and the division itself creates the landlocked condition.
source_note: Easement by necessity -- implied easement for landlocked parcels

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: For many years, a neighbor has openly, continuously, and without permission used a well-worn footpath across a portion of an adjoining owner's land to reach a lake, satisfying the applicable statutory time period. This may give rise to what type of easement?
choice_a: An easement created solely by a written deed
explanation: An easement by prescription arises, similar to adverse possession, when someone uses another's land openly, continuously, and without the owner's permission for the period of time required by state law, resulting in a legally recognized right to continue that specific use even though no deed ever granted it.
source_note: Easement by prescription (analogous to adverse possession)

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A homeowner gives a neighbor casual, revocable permission to walk across her backyard as a shortcut, without any formal written grant. This type of permission is best classified as what?
choice_b: An easement in gross that runs with the land
choice_c: A license, which is a personal, generally revocable permission rather than an interest in the land itself
explanation: A license is mere personal permission to use another's land for a specific purpose. Unlike an easement, a license does not create a permanent property interest, does not run with the land, and can generally be revoked by the landowner at will.
source_note: License distinguished from an easement -- revocable personal permission

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: During a routine boundary survey performed before closing, the buyer's surveyor discovers that the neighbor's garage roofline extends two feet over the property line onto the parcel being purchased. What is this condition called?
explanation: An encroachment occurs when a structure or improvement from one property unlawfully extends across the boundary line onto an adjoining owner's land without permission. Unlike an easement, which is an authorized use of another's land, an encroachment is an unauthorized intrusion typically uncovered by a boundary survey.
source_note: Encroachment -- unauthorized structural intrusion across a boundary line

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: What is the essential legal distinction between an easement and an encroachment?
choice_a: An easement is an authorized right to use another's land, while an encroachment is an unauthorized physical intrusion onto another's land
choice_b: There is no distinction; the terms mean the same thing
choice_c: An easement always involves a structure, while an encroachment never does
choice_d: An encroachment always benefits the burdened property's owner
explanation: An easement is a legally authorized, non-possessory right to use a portion of someone else's property (for access, utilities, etc.), while an encroachment is an unauthorized physical intrusion by a structure or improvement across a boundary onto a neighbor's land, typically without permission and often unintentional.
source_note: Distinction between an authorized easement and an unauthorized encroachment

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: Two adjoining homeowners share a single wall built exactly on the boundary line separating their two row houses, and each has rights to use and maintain that shared wall. What is this type of shared structure called?
explanation: A party wall is a wall situated on or along the boundary line between two adjoining properties, shared and used by both owners (common in attached row houses and townhomes), typically governed by a party wall easement or agreement setting out each owner's rights and maintenance obligations.
source_note: Party wall -- shared boundary wall easement

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A subdivision's recorded declaration privately requires that all homes be built with a minimum of 2,000 square feet and prohibits fences over four feet tall, even though the local zoning ordinance imposes no such requirements. What kind of land use control is this?
explanation: Deed restrictions (restrictive covenants) are private land use controls created by a developer or property owners and recorded against the land, separate and apart from public zoning. They can impose additional requirements stricter than zoning, and are typically enforced by other property owners in the development rather than by the government.
source_note: Private deed restrictions (restrictive covenants) distinguished from public zoning

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A zoning ordinance requires that any new home be built at least 25 feet back from the front property line and 10 feet from each side property line. What is this minimum required distance from a lot line called?
explanation: A setback is the minimum required distance a structure must be located from a property's front, rear, or side lot lines, as established by a zoning ordinance or building code, generally intended to control density, preserve light and air, and maintain neighborhood character.
source_note: Setback requirements under zoning ordinances

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: An appraiser determines that a commercially zoned corner lot currently used for a small surface parking lot would generate substantially higher value if developed with a mixed-use retail and residential building, as permitted by the current zoning. What appraisal concept does this analysis illustrate?
explanation: Highest and best use is the reasonably probable and legal use of a property that is physically possible, appropriately supported, financially feasible, and results in the highest value among the alternative uses considered -- a foundational appraisal concept for evaluating land use and development potential.
source_note: Highest and best use concept (appraisal theory applied to property use)

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: In the government (rectangular) survey system, sections within a township are numbered in a serpentine (boustrophedon) pattern. Where does numbering begin, and in which section does it end?
choice_a: It begins in the southwest corner (Section 1) and ends in the northwest corner (Section 36)
choice_b: It begins in the northeast corner (Section 1) and ends in the southeast corner (Section 36)
choice_c: It begins in the center (Section 1) and spirals outward to Section 36 at a corner
choice_d: Numbering is randomly assigned by each county
explanation: Sections within a township are numbered beginning with Section 1 in the northeast corner, proceeding west across the top tier to Section 6, then dropping down and running east across the next tier, continuing in this back-and-forth (serpentine) pattern until ending at Section 36 in the southeast corner.
source_note: Government (rectangular) survey system -- serpentine section numbering pattern

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: Which of the following best distinguishes real property from personal property (chattel)?
choice_a: Real property is always more valuable than personal property
choice_b: Personal property can never be converted into real property under any circumstances
choice_c: Real property consists of land, and anything permanently affixed to or legally associated with it, along with the attendant bundle of ownership rights; personal property is movable and not permanently attached to the land
choice_d: Only real property can be bought or sold
explanation: Real property includes land, permanent improvements, and fixtures, together with the legal bundle of ownership rights, while personal property (chattel) is movable property not permanently attached to real estate. Personal property can become real property through affixation and satisfaction of the fixture tests, illustrating that the categories are not fixed forever.
source_note: Fundamental distinction between real property and personal property (chattel)

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, and Property Use
question: A parcel's legal description in a deed reads: "Beginning at the iron pin at the intersection of Elm Street and River Road, thence North 45 degrees East 200 feet, thence South 45 degrees East 150 feet, thence South 45 degrees West 200 feet, thence North 45 degrees West 150 feet to the point of beginning." What type of legal description is this?
explanation: This description is a classic metes and bounds description: it starts at an identifiable point of beginning (the iron pin) and defines the parcel's boundary through a sequence of compass directions (bearings) and distances that return to the starting point.
source_note: Metes and bounds legal description method -- example format
